key_bets: Electromagnetic launcher can achieve 60 km/s with macroscopic projectiles at commercial scale, despite being a 15-30× velocity extrapolation beyond existing 2-4 km/s defense railguns with no industrial precedent
Proprietary 'amplifier' target design with multiple internal cavities achieves 200-1000× fusion gain via successive shockwave amplification, vs. NIF's current world record of ~4×
Flowing 1-meter-thick liquid lithium curtain simultaneously serves as first wall, tritium breeder (TBR 1.8), and heat capture medium while surviving repetitive blast loading at sub-Hz rep rates
Sub-Hz repetition rate (0.011-0.1 Hz) is sufficient for commercial power output because each high-gain shot delivers proportionally more fusion energy
Driver operational lifetime (barrel bore erosion at 60 km/s, sabot degradation, capacitor cycling) supports ~10⁸ shots over 40-year plant life without economically prohibitive replacement cycles
Mass manufacturing of 1.5-4.3 million precision multi-cavity targets per year is achievable at a per-target cost below the Goodin economic bound (~$10/target)
Tritium breeding ratio of 1.8 (independently validated by TÜV SÜD UK) enables 25 kg/year tritium surplus and fast self-sufficiency, sidestepping the D-T fleet-scaling bottleneck
eliminated_costs: Superconducting magnets entirely eliminated (no HTS coils, cryostats, or current leads) — removes 30-50% of conventional tokamak reactor plant cost
Precision beam optics and final optics survivability concerns absent (unlike laser ICF where final optics TRL ~2 is a dominant challenge)
Hohlraum target component eliminated (saves $1k-$10k per target vs. laser indirect-drive ICF Au/U hohlraums)
Vessel replacement eliminated — flowing liquid Li curtain protects structural vessel for plant lifetime (vs. periodic solid first-wall/blanket replacement in tokamaks)
Plasma disruption mitigation hardware unnecessary — no plasma exists to disrupt
novel_costs: Electromagnetic launcher capital cost — entirely uncharacterized for 60 km/s, 100 MJ class device with no industrial or defense analogue (likely dominant CAPEX item)

Per-shot consumable structure absent from all conventional plant cost models — 1.5-4.3M precision multi-cavity targets/year plus projectiles destroyed each shot, forming a recurring CAPEX-like cost with no standard CAS slot

Driver operational lifetime replacement costs — barrel bore erosion at 60 km/s is an extreme wear regime with no empirical precedent; replacement frequency could span 4 orders of magnitude (10⁵ to 10⁹ shots)

Flowing liquid lithium chamber engineering — pumps, inert-atmosphere containment for chemically reactive Li, blast-resistant curtain geometry, and Li-to-steam pulsed heat exchanger have no operating-plant analogues
Lithium-6 enrichment cost premium — if natural Li insufficient for TBR 1.8, enriched Li adds $143-$451M/reactor vs. $70M for natural Li (2-6× cost premium plus supply chain constraints)

risks.description: Target gain at 60 km/s never experimentally tested — Machine 4 cancelled February 2025 before the critical velocity-scaling experiment; the entire commercial concept rests on extrapolating from ~50 neutrons at 6.5 km/s (Machine 3, 2022) to 200-1000× gain at 60 km/s, a multi-order-of-magnitude leap

Electromagnetic gun capital cost is a deeply uncertain free parameter with no published analogue; FLARE pivot (Sept 2025) is indirect evidence FLF's own analysis found projectile driver cost incompatible with <$50/MWh viability threshold

Concept has been provisionally abandoned by its primary developer (First Light Fusion pivoted to FLARE pulsed-power liner implosion in September 2025); no active commercial pursuer of pure projectile ICF remains

Driver operational lifetime spans 4 orders of magnitude in plausible range (10⁵ to 10⁹ shots); Hawker (2020) shows driver lifetime is a stronger LCOE lever (Pearson −0.134) than driver capital cost (+0.075), and barrel replacement every 10⁵ shots would impose ~1,300 replacement cycles over plant life

Flowing liquid lithium curtain is doubly load-bearing (first wall + sole tritium breeding system); if blast-loading dynamics, containment cost, or pump power prove unviable, both the vessel-lifetime advantage and TBR 1.8 surplus collapse together, requiring a solid blanket fallback that adds vessel replacement costs and pushes TBR down to 1.05-1.15

Rep rate × gain coupling creates a cliff-edge constraint — if gain falls below 200×, the rep rate required to maintain 333 MWe rises above 0.1 Hz, potentially violating the (unmeasured) chamber Li-curtain clearing time after blast

Mass manufacturing of 1.5-4.3 million precision multi-cavity 'amplifier' targets per year has no demonstrated analogue; defect tolerance, yield rates, positional tolerance requirements, and material composition (potential Au content) are all proprietary or uncharacterized

Tritium byproduct revenue (~$750M/year at current $30,000/g pricing, ~60% of electricity revenue) is structurally self-undermining — fleet deployment that produces multiple 25 kg/year surpluses would collapse tritium price toward marginal production cost; cannot be relied upon as base-case revenue
FLF's quoted repetition rates are inconsistent across public sources (10s, 30s, 90s between shots), spanning nearly a 10× range that propagates linearly into capital cost amortization uncertainty

NearStar Fusion (taxonomic comparator) is at NSF SBIR Phase I level with no peer-reviewed publications, no demonstrated fusion, and no cost estimates; their MTIF approach is taxonomically closer to MIF than pure projectile ICF

Lithium-6 enrichment requirement to achieve TBR 1.8 is unstated by FLF; if enriched Li is needed, costs rise from $70M to $143-$451M per reactor and supply chain becomes constrained (historically Russia/China-dominated capacity)

Driver wall-plug efficiency is unpublished, making the recirculating power fraction uncertain; combined with unquantified Li pump power (rough HYLIFE analogue suggests 1-2% but FLF chamber geometry differs), engineering Q remains uncharacterized
